opus-5.5.text:
I think the core issue is that a benchmark is a fixed distribution, and once a field starts optimizing toward it, whether explicitly or implicitly, the number stops telling you what you actually care about. For chatbots that was already a problem, but for agents it's much more serious.

An agent's value comes from handling long, open-ended tasks in environments it hasn't seen before. You give it a goal, it has to explore, use tools, recover from mistakes, and decide when it's done. A benchmark usually freezes a set of environments, tools, and success criteria. So what you end up measuring is how well the model performs on that particular slice of the world, not whether it has learned a transferable skill. And because so much training now happens in RL environments, it's very easy, sometimes without even meaning to, to build training environments that look a lot like the evaluation. Then the score goes up, but the generalization doesn't necessarily come with it.

There's also a horizon problem. Many benchmarks are still relatively short tasks with clean verification. Real agentic work might involve hundreds of steps, ambiguous feedback, and a world that changes while you're acting in it. The capabilities that matter there, like long-term planning, self-correction, and knowing what you don't know, are hard to capture in a single pass/fail metric.

So the way I think about it is that benchmarks are necessary but not sufficient. They're good for catching regressions and making coarse comparisons. But to judge whether an agent really generalizes, you have to look at how it performs on genuinely new tasks, ideally ones that real users bring, in distributions nobody tuned for. In some sense, the real benchmark is whether people actually use it to get real work done. That signal is noisier, but it's much harder to overfit.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmark scores can rise without transferable capability and that real user work is a harder-to-overfit measure, conveying that benchmark optimization may not yield an agent that works well for users.

r002.rationale: It says benchmarks measure performance on a fixed slice of the world and that gains do not necessarily transfer to unseen environments or genuinely new tasks.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the core issue is that a benchmark is, by construction, a closed distribution. Someone sits down, defines a task space, writes a few hundred or a few thousand problems, and freezes it. The moment that happens, you've created something that can be optimized against directly. And once the whole field is optimizing against it, the score stops measuring the thing the benchmark was originally meant to proxy for. It starts measuring how well you've fit the benchmark.

With agents this gets worse than with ordinary language models, because what we actually care about with an agent is behavior in an open environment. Can it handle a tool it's never seen? Can it recover when a step fails in a way that wasn't anticipated? Can it figure out the right next action when the task description is underspecified, which is how real tasks almost always arrive? None of that is captured well by a fixed set of trajectories with known answers. You can get a very high score on an agent benchmark and still have a model that falls apart the moment the environment deviates slightly from what it saw in training.

There's also a contamination problem, which is subtle. Even if you're careful not to train on the test set, the structure of the benchmark leaks. The style of the tasks, the kinds of tools, the typical length of a solution. Teams build training data that looks like the benchmark, and the model learns the shape of the benchmark rather than the underlying capability. So the gap between benchmark performance and real generalization quietly widens over time, and the benchmark itself can't tell you that's happening.

So for us, benchmarks are useful as a sanity check and as a way to catch regressions. But if you want to know whether an agent actually generalizes, you have to put it in environments it wasn't built for, with tasks that keep changing, and look at what it does. That's harder and messier, and the numbers are less clean. But I'd rather have a messy signal about the right thing than a clean signal about the wrong thing.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmark optimization may not reflect real-world agent capability, but it does not state that this leads to a poor user experience.

r002.rationale: It says an agent can score highly on a fixed benchmark yet fall apart when the environment deviates from what it saw in training.

astra-6.text:
I think benchmarks are useful, but they usually measure generalization within a fairly narrow distribution. You have a fixed set of tasks, a particular environment, and a clear scoring rule. An agent can perform very well there without being able to handle a new situation where the tools are different, the goal is ambiguous, or it has to recover from a mistake.

For agents, that gap becomes especially important because they interact with the environment. Each action changes what they see next, so a small error can lead them into a situation that the benchmark never anticipated. Getting individual steps right isn’t necessarily the same as reliably completing a long task.

And once everyone optimizes against the same benchmark, it becomes harder to distinguish broad capability from adaptation to that particular test. So I would want to evaluate agents across changing environments and genuinely new tasks, with limited task-specific tuning. The question is whether the agent can adapt and accomplish the user’s goal when the conditions are different from what we prepared it for.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmark success may not translate to reliably completing long tasks or accomplishing the user’s goal under different conditions, but it does not clearly state that this can result in a poor user experience.

r002.rationale: The response says benchmark performance may not transfer to new situations, changing environments, or conditions different from those prepared for, directly identifying out-of-distribution failures.

sol-6.1.text:
I think benchmarks give us a useful signal, but they only sample a small part of what an agent might encounter. If you repeatedly optimize against a fixed set of tasks, it becomes difficult to distinguish generalization from adaptation to that particular evaluation.

For agents, the challenge is also more than producing a correct answer. An agent needs to make decisions over many steps, use feedback, and recover when something unexpected happens. A system might perform well in a controlled benchmark but struggle when the tools, environment, or user’s requirements change.

So I would look at benchmarks alongside performance on new tasks and in changing environments. Can the agent handle a situation that wasn’t anticipated by the people who designed the test? Can it recognize a mistake and adjust? Those are important parts of generalization that a single benchmark score can miss.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmark optimization may hide weaknesses in multi-step decisions, feedback, and recovery, but it does not state that this can lead to a poor user experience.

r002.rationale: It states that an agent may struggle when tools, environments, or user requirements change, and asks whether it can handle situations the test designers did not anticipate.
